ukmt-pink-2019-14.title: Count the arcs
ukmt-pink-2019-14.body:
Join each centre to the points where the circles meet. Every circle passes through the centres of its neighbours, so the triangles formed are equilateral and all the angles are $60^\circ$.

Each outer circle loses an arc of $120^\circ$ (one third of its circumference) where it overlaps the middle circle, so $\frac23$ of each outer circle remains. The middle circle contributes the two arcs at top and bottom of $60^\circ$ each, i.e. $\frac13$ of its circumference. Total $\frac23+\frac23+\frac13=\frac53$ circumferences.

Perimeter $=\frac53\times2\pi R=\frac{10\pi R}{3}$.

**Answer: (C)**

ukmt-pink-2019-17.title: Fold the net
ukmt-pink-2019-17.body:
The four triangles on the left fold into a square-based pyramid without its base, and the four on the right fold into another one. The two pyramids are hinged along the dashed edge between them. When they are folded together to close the octahedron, the free end of the edge marked $x$ meets the end of the edge marked $E$, so $x$ coincides with $E$.

**Answer: (E)**

ukmt-pink-2019-19.title: Find where the triples start
ukmt-pink-2019-19.body:
The 9 one-digit numbers use 9 digits, so the triples start at positions $1,4,7,10,\dots$ (positions $\equiv1 \pmod 3$). The tens digit of the two-digit number $n$ is at position $2n-10$ and its units digit is at position $2n-9$.

A triple starts at the tens digit of $n$ when $2n-10\equiv1\pmod 3$, that is $n\equiv1\pmod3$. It then reads: tens digit of $n$, units digit of $n$, tens digit of $n+1$.
- $n=22$: (222). $n=43$: (434). $n=46$: (464). $n=88$: (888). All are possible triples.

A triple starts at the units digit of $n$ when $n\equiv2\pmod3$; it reads: units digit of $n$, tens and units digits of $n+1$. For $n=77\equiv 2$ this gives (778) (and $n=76\equiv1$ gives (767)). So the digits 7,7,7 never form a triple.

**Answer: (D) (777)**

ukmt-pink-2019-24.title: Compare areas using $\frac12ab\sin C$
ukmt-pink-2019-24.body:
Let $u$ be the area of $JLM$ and $v$ the area of $JMK$. Since $M$ is the midpoint of $KL$, $u=v=\frac12S$.

$\angle QJR=\angle KJM$ (vertically opposite) with $JR=4JK$ and $JQ=3JM$, so area $JQR=3\times4\times v=6S$. Similarly area $PJQ=2\times3\times u=3S$ and area $JPR=2\times4\times S=8S$.

The point $J$ lies outside triangle $PQR$, and triangles $PJQ$ and $JQR$ have the same orientation as $PQR$ while $JRP$ has the opposite one. So $[PQR]=[PJQ]+[JQR]-[JRP]=3S+6S-8S=S$.

**Answer: (A) $S$**

ukmt-pink-2019-24.title: Coordinates with vectors
ukmt-pink-2019-24.body:
Put $J$ at the origin, $K=\mathbf k$, $L=\mathbf l$, so $S=\frac12|\mathbf k\times\mathbf l|$. Then $P=-2\mathbf l$, $Q=-\frac32(\mathbf k+\mathbf l)$, $R=-4\mathbf k$.

$Q-P=-\frac32\mathbf k+\frac12\mathbf l$ and $R-P=-4\mathbf k+2\mathbf l$, so $(Q-P)\times(R-P)=-3\,\mathbf k\times\mathbf l+2\,\mathbf k\times\mathbf l=-\mathbf k\times\mathbf l$.

Hence $[PQR]=\frac12|\mathbf k\times\mathbf l|=S$.

**Answer: (A) $S$**
